docs.title: What is fjc-idb?
docs.text: fjc-idb turns the Federal Judicial Center's Integrated Database (IDB) into clean CSV files.

docs.title: Why use fjc-idb?
docs.text:
• Readable columns. IDB field names such as PROCPROG become descriptive names such as procedural_progress, and codes become labels from the FJC codebooks (Ninth Circuit, Dismissed as settled, Los Angeles, CA).
  • Correct missing data. The IDB's missing-value codes (-8 and the date 1900-01-01) become real missing values, with the exceptions the codebooks describe (such as civil in forma pauperis status, where -8 means "no").
  • No double counting. Each yearly file repeats every case still pending when it was made. fjc-idb keeps pending cases only from the latest file, so combining years does not count a case more than once.
  • Useful added columns. Indicators for appeal types and for groups of offenses and natures of suit, the days between key dates, counts of concurrences and dissents, a standard appellate docket number, and more.
  • Large files, little memory. Years are processed one at a time, so even the criminal files (144 columns) need only a gigabyte or two of memory.
  • Codebooks for the output. The documentation includes codebooks that describe every column of the CSV files and how it relates to the IDB.

The IDB is the most complete public source of case-level data on the federal courts, but it is distributed as one SAS file per year with confusing field names and a messy coding system. This repo addresses those shortcomings. But it cannot cure the issue of missing data (particularly judge names). However, the improvements made here should make it easier to merge the IDB data with other sources (using the standard docket number format in docket_number).

fjc-idb has been tested on the files from 2008 through 2026. It does not yet support the bankruptcy files or the older files that use older codebooks.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Python 3.11 or later
  • An internet connection to download the IDB files from the FJC IDB page, or the SAS (.sas7bdat) files themselves

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
To install fjc-idb, use pip:

pip install fjc-idb

The package is installed as fjc-idb and imported in Python as fjc_idb:

import fjc_idb

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
Download the yearly files from the FJC website and export them in one step:

fjc-idb appellate --start-year 2008 --stop-year 2026 --data-folder path/to/fjc_idb --download

--download fetches only the files the data folder does not already have, along with the FJC codebook for each case type. Use --download-only to fetch files without exporting, and --overwrite to replace files already downloaded (the FJC updates the file for the current year during the year). Once the files are downloaded, leave out --download to export them again:

fjc-idb all --start-year 2015 --data-folder path/to/fjc_idb

Or from Python:

import fjc_idb

fjc_idb.download('criminal', 2008, 2026, data_folder = 'path/to/fjc_idb')
fjc_idb.run('criminal', 2008, 2026, data_folder = 'path/to/fjc_idb')

The files are saved in this layout under their FJC names (such as ap08.sas7bdat or cv12_0.sas7bdat). Files you download yourself work the same way if you put them in the same folders:

fjc_idb/
├── appellate/          ap08.sas7bdat, ap09.sas7bdat, ...
├── district/
│   ├── civil/          cv08_0.sas7bdat, cv09_0.sas7bdat, ...
│   └── criminal/       cr08.sas7bdat, cr09.sas7bdat, ...
└── docs/               the FJC codebooks

Each case type is saved next to its yearly files as fjc_idb_{case_type}_data_{start_year}_{stop_year}.csv. Missing dates are written as NA, and other missing values are left blank.

Option Default Description case types (required) appellate, civil, criminal, or all --start-year (required) The first statistical year to include --stop-year the current year The last statistical year to include --data-folder set in options.py The folder with the IDB files --rename-columns true Use descriptive column names, or false to keep the IDB field names --fix-city-spellings true Correct misspelled city names, or false to keep the FJC codebook spellings --download off Download missing files from the FJC website before exporting --download-only off Download missing files without exporting --overwrite off Replace files that were already downloaded --merge-district off Also merge the appellate data with the matching civil and criminal district records

See the documentation for a tutorial, codebooks for each case type, and example analyses.

docs.title: Command line options
docs.text:
fjc-idb CASE_TYPE [CASE_TYPE ...] --start-year YEAR [options]
Option Default Description CASE_TYPE (required) One or more of appellate, civil, and criminal, or all. --start-year (required) The first statistical year to include. --stop-year the current year The last statistical year to include. --data-folder options._DATA_FOLDER The data folder, laid out as in the Tutorial. --rename-columns [true\|false] options._RENAME_COLUMNS (true) Whether to use descriptive column names (true) or keep the IDB field names (false). --fix-city-spellings [true\|false] options._FIX_CITY_SPELLINGS (true) Whether to correct the twelve city names misspelled in the FJC codebook (true) or keep them (false). --download off Download files missing from the data folder before exporting. --download-only off Download files missing from the data folder without exporting. --overwrite off With --download or --download-only, replace files that already exist. --merge-district off After exporting, merge the appellate data with the civil and criminal district data (see Merging appellate and district data).

The export options are arguments of fjc_idb.run and the functions in fjc_idb.main, and the download options are arguments of fjc_idb.download.

docs.title: Downloading
docs.text:
fjc_idb.download reads the FJC dataset page for a case type, finds the link for each requested year, and saves the file in the data folder. Only the files for single years are used, not the cumulative, five- and ten-year, or twelve-months-ending-June files on the same pages, and bankruptcy data is not included.

  • Folders. Any folders of the data folder that do not exist yet are created first, for every case type and the docs folder. Use fjc_idb.create_folders to create them without downloading.
  • Existing files. A year is skipped if the data folder already has a file for it. With overwrite, the new file is downloaded first and then any older file for the year is removed, so a failed download never loses data.
  • Partial downloads. Files are written under a temporary .part name and renamed when complete.
  • Missing years. Years the FJC has not published are skipped with a warning.
  • Codebooks. The codebook linked from each dataset page is saved in the docs folder of the data folder (pass codebook = False to skip it).

The dataset pages are listed in options._DATASET_PAGES. If the FJC moves a page, update its address there.

docs.title: Merging appellate and district data
docs.text:
fjc_idb.merge_district (or --merge-district) adds the district court's record of each appealed case to the appellate data and saves the result in the appellate folder as fjc_idb_appellate_with_district_data_{start_year}_{stop_year}.csv. It needs the appellate, civil, and criminal files for the same years.

import fjc_idb

merged = fjc_idb.merge_district(2008, 2026, data_folder = 'path/to/fjc_idb')

How appeals are matched.

  • An appeal is matched with the civil or criminal data according to its appeal type (rules.district_civil_appeal_types and rules.district_criminal_appeal_types). This matters because a district can give a civil case and a criminal case the same docket number.
  • Civil appeals are matched by district and docket number. Criminal appeals are matched by district, docket number, and defendant number; an appeal without a defendant number is matched only if the docket has a single defendant.
  • A reopened, remanded, or transferred case can have several district records with the same docket number. The appeal is matched with the latest record filed on or before the notice of appeal or, if none was, with the latest record.
  • Administrative appeals, original proceedings, and appeals from bankruptcy courts and bankruptcy appellate panels have no district record and are not matched.

Columns. The district columns are added with the prefix district_, such as district_filing_date, district_disposition, or district_prison_total_months. Columns that civil and criminal records share (such as the filing and termination dates) are combined into one column. Columns that only repeat the match keys or the appellate data are left out; they are listed in rules.redundant_civil_columns and rules.redundant_criminal_columns. The added district_match column is civil or criminal for a matched appeal and blank otherwise.

Coverage. A district case is in the district files only if it was terminated in the range of years or was still pending, so appeals filed long after the start year match far more often than early ones. For 2008 through 2026, 93% of civil appeals and 80% of criminal appeals were matched (98% and 88% of those filed in 2010 or later). The merged data always uses the descriptive column names.

The merge reads the civil and criminal files one year at a time and keeps only the records of appealed cases. For 2008 through 2026 it takes about as long as exporting all three case types.

docs.title: Changing the defaults
docs.text:
The defaults live in src/fjc_idb/options.py and apply to the Python functions and the command line alike.

Option Default Description _DATA_FOLDER data/courts/fjc_idb, four folders above options.py The data folder. _RENAME_COLUMNS True Whether to rename columns. _FIX_CITY_SPELLINGS True Whether to correct misspelled city names. _DATE_FORMAT %Y-%m-%d How dates are written to the CSV files. _DATASET_PAGES the FJC dataset pages The web page that links to the yearly files for each case type. _DOWNLOAD_TIMEOUT 300 Seconds to wait for the FJC website before a download fails. _ENCODING latin-1 The text encoding of the SAS files. _MISSING_CODES ('-8', -8) Codes treated as missing when combining district and office codes and when building indicator columns. _MISSING_DATE 1900-01-01 The date the IDB uses for missing dates. _PENDING_COLUMN, _PENDING_YEAR TAPEYEAR, 2099 The column and value that mark pending records.

docs.title: How the pipeline works
docs.text:
fjc_idb.run processes one yearly file at a time:

  1. Import. The yearly SAS file is read. Pending records are dropped from every file except the latest one, because a pending case is repeated in each file until it ends.
  2. Prepare. Columns that depend on the raw codes are added (such as indicator columns and docket_number), and district and office codes are combined with their circuit and district so that they match the codebook.
  3. Parse. Each column is cleaned according to its Column specification: missing-value codes become missing data, codes are replaced by labels, and the column is converted to its data type. City spellings are corrected and the days between key dates are added.
  4. Rename. Columns get their descriptive names.
  5. Export. The rows are appended to the CSV file, with missing data written as each column's missing_replacement.

Because only one year is in memory at a time, even the criminal files (144 columns, about 1.7 million defendants for 2008–2026) need only one to two gigabytes. import_data and parse_data work on a whole range at once and are useful for short ranges or interactive work.

docs.title: Customizing columns
docs.text:
Each case type has a dictionary of Column instances in fjc_idb.base (appellate_columns, civil_columns, and criminal_columns), keyed by the column's new name. A Column describes how to parse one IDB field:

Column(
    'JUDGMENT',                 # the IDB field name
    'judgment_for',             # the new column name
    str,                        # str, int, or 'date'
    missing_value = ['-8', '0'],  # code(s) meaning missing, or None
    missing_replacement = '',   # what to write for missing data
    decoder = rules.judgments)  # labels that replace the codes

To change how a column is parsed, edit its entry. For example, to keep the codebook's -8 in class_action instead of leaving it blank:

'class_action': Column('CLASSACT', 'class_action', int, missing_value = None),

docs.title: Customizing rules
docs.text:
The fjc_idb.rules package holds the code lists and labels, divided into modules by case type:

Module Contents rules.courts Circuits, districts, courthouses, city spelling fixes, the date gaps added to every file, and the rules for merging appellate and district data rules.appellate Appeal types, agencies, writs, publication, and other appellate labels rules.offenses Groups of criminal offense codes, shared by the appellate and criminal files rules.civil Groups of nature of suit codes, jurisdiction labels, and civil district labels rules.criminal Criminal district labels

Every rule is also available directly from fjc_idb.rules, such as rules.circuits.

docs.title: Adding an indicator column
docs.text:
Indicator columns come from dictionaries that map a column name to a list of codes. To add an offense group, define the list in rules/offenses.py and add it to criminal_offense_columns:

criminal_bank_robbery: list[str] = ['1100']

criminal_offense_columns: dict[str, list[str]] = {
    ...
    'criminal_bank_robbery': criminal_bank_robbery}

The new column then appears in both the appellate and criminal files. Nature of suit groups work the same way through civil_nature_of_suit_columns in rules/civil.py.

docs.title: Adding a date gap
docs.text:
rules.date_gaps maps a new column name to a pair of IDB date fields. A gap is added to every file that has both fields:

date_gaps: dict[str, tuple[str, str]] = {
    ...
    'filing_to_sentencing': ('FILEDATE', 'SENTDATE')}

docs.title: Notes on the data
docs.text:
• Statistical years. Since 1993, the statistical year has matched the federal fiscal year (October 1 through September 30).
  • Updated records. Each record is the latest version the FJC received, so values that changed during a case (such as pro se status or the charges) can be overwritten. The FJC's research guide recommends saving each quarterly update to keep the full history.
  • Data quality. Fields used in the AO's published tables have quality checks; others, such as pro se status, in forma pauperis status, and class action allegations, do not.
  • Judges. Judge codes are blank in the public files under Judicial Conference policy.

docs.title: Style Guidelines
docs.text:
This package follows the Google Python Style Guide with two notable exceptions:

  1. It always adds spaces around "=". This not only violates the Google guide, it violates PEP8, the foundational Python style guide from which all other resources are derived. I defy this strong, long-standing norm because I find it more readable. My brain and eyes have trouble seeing two separate objects when an equal sign is in the middle. I imagine that I am not alone in this accessibility issue. Further, as PEP8 itself notes, required spaces around equal signs are becoming increasing common with type annotations becoming part of best practices (and, as a result, signatures to classes, functions, and methods regularly include spaces around the equal signs). I realize that this will seem alien to many coders, but it is far easier on my eyes.
  2. I use some so-called "power features", primarily dunder methods, to make my interfaces easier to access and use. This is disfavored in the Google Python Style Guide because such code is often more difficult for others to read. To address that concern, I try to document and comment as to what the code is doing whenever I used any of the "power features" of Python.

Because of the first exception, the project does not use a code formatter (such as ruff format), which would remove those spaces.

docs.title: Recipes
docs.text: These examples use pandas to analyze the CSV files that fjc-idb creates. They assume the files were exported for 2008 through 2026 into the default data folder; change the paths to match your own files.

docs.title: Load a CSV file with the right types
docs.text:
fjc-idb writes missing dates as NA and leaves other missing values blank. Because a few party names are literally "NA", read NA as missing only in date columns. The column specifications in fjc_idb.base say which columns are dates:

import pandas as pd

from fjc_idb import base, options


def load_csv(path, case_type, columns = None):
    """Loads an fjc-idb CSV file with missing data and dates parsed."""
    specs = getattr(base, f'{case_type}_columns').values()
    dates = [spec.name for spec in specs if spec.data_type == 'date']
    header = pd.read_csv(path, nrows = 0).columns
    columns = columns or list(header)
    na_values = {
        column: ['', 'NA'] if column in dates else [''] for column in columns}
    return pd.read_csv(
        path,
        usecols = columns,
        keep_default_na = False,
        na_values = na_values,
        parse_dates = [column for column in columns if column in dates],
        low_memory = False)


folder = options._DATA_FOLDER
appeals = load_csv(
    folder / 'appellate' / 'fjc_idb_appellate_data_2008_2026.csv', 'appellate')

The civil and criminal files are large (2.2 GB and 1.3 GB for 2008–2026), so pass columns to load only what you need.

docs.title: Affirmance rate by circuit
docs.text:
disposition holds the outcome of appeals decided on the merits, which are the appeals with when_terminated 1 or 2 (code 1 in disposition is affirmed).

merits = appeals[appeals['when_terminated'].isin([1, 2])]
affirmed = (merits['disposition'] == 1).groupby(merits['circuit']).mean()
affirmed.sort_values()

docs.title: Share of decisions published each year
docs.text:
terminated = appeals[appeals['pending'] == 0]
terminated.groupby('data_file_year')['published'].mean()

docs.title: Time from notice of appeal to judgment
docs.text: appeals.groupby('circuit')['notice_to_judgment'].median().sort_values()

docs.title: Appeals with a dissent
docs.text:
decided = appeals[appeals['dissents'].notna()]
(decided['dissents'] > 0).groupby(decided['circuit']).mean()

docs.title: Conviction rate by offense group
docs.text:
disposition_1 is the defendant's final disposition. The offense group columns mark the groups of any of the defendant's five charges at filing.

criminal = load_csv(
    folder / 'district' / 'criminal' / 'fjc_idb_criminal_data_2008_2026.csv',
    'criminal',
    ['pending', 'disposition_1', 'criminal_drugs', 'criminal_firearms',
     'criminal_immigration', 'criminal_fraud'])
closed = criminal[criminal['pending'] == 0]
convicted = closed['disposition_1'].str.startswith('Convicted', na = False)
groups = [
    'criminal_drugs', 'criminal_firearms', 'criminal_immigration',
    'criminal_fraud']
pd.Series({group: convicted[closed[group] == 1].mean() for group in groups})

docs.title: Count defendants filed each fiscal year
docs.text:
The AO counts a defendant as filed in the fiscal year of the proceeding date. A fiscal year starts on October 1, so October through December belong to the next year:

filings = load_csv(
    folder / 'district' / 'criminal' / 'fjc_idb_criminal_data_2008_2026.csv',
    'criminal',
    ['proceeding_date', 'reopen_sequence'])
filings = filings[filings['reopen_sequence'] == 0]
date = filings['proceeding_date']
fiscal_year = date.dt.year + (date.dt.month >= 10)
filings.groupby(fiscal_year).size().loc[2008:]

The count_* columns (such as count_filed) describe the fiscal year of the file each record came from. Because fjc-idb keeps each defendant only from the latest file that includes it, summing those columns by year undercounts defendants who were still pending at the end of an earlier year.

docs.title: Settlement rate by nature of suit group
docs.text:
civil = load_csv(
    folder / 'district' / 'civil' / 'fjc_idb_civil_data_2008_2026.csv',
    'civil',
    ['pending', 'disposition', 'civil_civil_rights', 'civil_habeas',
     'civil_ip', 'civil_social_security'])
closed = civil[civil['pending'] == 0]
settled = closed['disposition'] == 'Dismissed as settled'
groups = [
    'civil_civil_rights', 'civil_habeas', 'civil_ip', 'civil_social_security']
pd.Series({group: settled[closed[group] == 1].mean() for group in groups})

docs.title: Work with the data in Python instead of CSV files
docs.text:
To skip the CSV files, import and parse the data directly. The whole range is held in memory, so use short ranges for civil and criminal data:

from fjc_idb import main, options

folder = options._DATA_FOLDER / 'district' / 'criminal'
raw = main.import_data('criminal', 2025, 2026, folder)
criminal = main.parse_data(raw, 'criminal')

docs.title: Tutorial
docs.text: This tutorial walks through downloading the FJC Integrated Database (IDB) files and turning them into clean CSV files.

docs.title: 1. Install fjc-idb
docs.text:
fjc-idb requires Python 3.11 or later.

pip install fjc-idb

The package is installed as fjc-idb and imported in Python as fjc_idb:

import fjc_idb

To work from a copy of the repository instead, install it with uv:

uv sync

docs.title: 2. Choose a data folder
docs.text:
fjc-idb keeps the IDB files, the FJC codebooks, and the CSV files it creates in one data folder with this layout:

fjc_idb/                  <- the data folder
├── appellate/
│   ├── ap08.sas7bdat
│   └── ...
├── district/
│   ├── civil/
│   │   ├── cv08_0.sas7bdat
│   │   └── ...
│   └── criminal/
│       ├── cr08.sas7bdat
│       └── ...
└── docs/                 <- the FJC codebooks

Pass the location of this folder with --data-folder (or data_folder in Python), or set it once as the default in options.py (see the Advanced User Guide). The folder and its subfolders do not need to exist yet: downloading creates any that are missing, and fjc_idb.create_folders('path/to/fjc_idb') creates them without downloading anything.

docs.title: 3. Download the IDB files
docs.text:
fjc-idb downloads the yearly SAS files from the FJC IDB page and saves them in the data folder under their FJC names. It covers the three datasets that fjc-idb parses; bankruptcy data is not included.

Case type FJC dataset Years available appellate Appellate cases filed, terminated, and pending, FY 2008 to present 2008 on civil Civil cases filed, terminated, and pending, SY 1988 to present 1988 on criminal Criminal defendants filed, terminated, and pending, FY 1996 to present 1996 on

From the command line:

fjc-idb appellate --start-year 2008 --stop-year 2026 --data-folder path/to/fjc_idb --download-only

Or from Python:

import fjc_idb

fjc_idb.download('appellate', 2008, 2026, data_folder = 'path/to/fjc_idb')

Files that are already in the data folder are skipped, so running the command again only fetches what is missing. The codebook for each case type is saved in docs/. The file for the current year is updated by the FJC during the year; add --overwrite (or overwrite = True) to replace it with the latest version. To see which years the FJC publishes, use fjc_idb.list_files:

fjc_idb.list_files('criminal')   # {1996: 'https://www.fjc.gov/...', ...}

The files are large: about 14 MB per year for appellate data, 60 to 180 MB per year for civil data, and 160 to 200 MB per year for criminal data.

Downloading the files yourself

You can also download the files from the FJC website by hand. Keep their names as they are (the FJC sometimes adds a suffix, as in ap12_0.sas7bdat) and put them in the folders shown above.

docs.title: 4. Export the data
docs.text:
From the command line, give the case types and the first year to include:

fjc-idb appellate --start-year 2008 --stop-year 2026 --data-folder path/to/fjc_idb

python -m fjc_idb works the same way. Use all for every case type, and add --download to fetch any missing files first:

fjc-idb all --start-year 2008 --data-folder path/to/fjc_idb --download

Or, from Python:

import fjc_idb

fjc_idb.run('appellate', 2008, 2026, data_folder = 'path/to/fjc_idb')

Each case type is saved next to its yearly files, for example appellate/fjc_idb_appellate_data_2008_2026.csv. When no stop year is given, the current year is used. For 2008 through 2026, the appellate file takes about a minute, the civil file about five minutes, and the criminal file about seven.

To add the district court record of each appealed case to the appellate data, add --merge-district (or call fjc_idb.merge_district). It needs the files for all three case types:

fjc-idb all --start-year 2008 --data-folder path/to/fjc_idb --merge-district

The merged data is saved as appellate/fjc_idb_appellate_with_district_data_2008_2026.csv. See the Advanced User Guide for how appeals are matched.

docs.title: 5. Understand the output
docs.text:
Each CSV file has one row per appeal, civil case, or criminal defendant, with:

  • descriptive column names in place of the IDB's short field names,
  • readable labels in place of many codes (for example, Ninth Circuit instead of 9),
  • missing data written as NA in date columns and left blank elsewhere,
  • added columns, such as indicators for groups of offenses and the number of days between key dates, and
  • pending cases taken only from the latest file in the range.

The codebooks in this User Guide describe every column:

  • Appellate Codebook
  • Criminal District Codebook
  • Civil District Codebook

docs.title: 6. Analyze the data
docs.text: See Recipes for loading the CSV files with pandas and for example analyses.

docs.title: Appellate Codebook
docs.text: This codebook describes the appellate CSV file that fjc-idb creates from the FJC Integrated Database (IDB) files for the U.S. courts of appeals. It follows the FJC's Appeals Documentation, FY 2008 – Present (revised February 10, 2021), adapted to the column names, labels, and added columns that fjc-idb produces. The original codebook is available from the FJC IDB page.

docs.title: About the data
docs.text:
• One row per appeal. Each row is an appeal docketed in a court of appeals. Docket numbers are unique only within a circuit, and an appeal that is reopened or remanded can appear again with a new row.
  • Years. The IDB has one file for each statistical year, which runs from October 1 through September 30 (statistical year 2026 began on October 1, 2025). Each file holds the appeals terminated that year. The most recent files also hold a snapshot of appeals still pending when the file was made.
  • Pending appeals. A pending appeal is repeated in each file until it ends, so fjc-idb keeps pending appeals only from the latest file in the range. In those rows, pending is 1 and data_file_year is 2099.
  • Column order. The CSV keeps the order of the original file, with each added column placed next to the column it comes from. The tables below group the columns by subject instead.

docs.title: Conventions
docs.text: Topic How fjc-idb handles it Column names Each original IDB field is renamed to a descriptive name. Pass rename_columns=False (or --rename-columns false) to keep the IDB names, such as CIRCUIT. Missing data The IDB code -8 and the date 1900-01-01 mean missing data. They are written as NA in date columns and left blank in all other columns, unless a column below says otherwise. Not applicable The IDB code -9 means a field does not apply (for example, a nature of suit for a criminal appeal). It is kept as -9 unless a column below says otherwise. Labels Columns marked with a label table have their codes replaced by labels. Codes with no label are kept as they are. Indicators Added indicator columns are 1 for yes and 0 for no. Added columns Columns marked added are created by fjc-idb and are not in the IDB.

docs.title: Case identification
docs.text: Column IDB field Type Description circuit CIRCUIT text Circuit in which the appeal was filed. See Circuits. docket_num_idb DOCKET text Docket number as stored in the IDB: a two-digit year and a serial number, with a 0 inserted before four-digit serial numbers (1701234 for 17-1234). Five-digit serial numbers have no inserted 0 (1910001). docket_number DOCKET text Added. The docket number in standard form, such as No. 17-1234. reopened_or_remanded REOPEN text Whether the appeal was reopened or remanded. See Reopened or remanded. Blank for appeals that were never reopened or remanded; the IDB codes these as missing. docket_date DKTDATE date Date the appeal was docketed in the court of appeals. data_file_year TAPEYEAR integer Statistical year of the file the row comes from: the year the appeal was terminated, or 2099 for pending appeals. pending STATUSCD integer 1 for a pending appeal (IDB code S) and 0 for a terminated appeal (L). new_filing TRANSCODE integer Type of the last transaction on the record: 1 for a new filing (E) and 0 for a change to an existing record, including its termination (J). The undocumented code R, which appears on a few pending appeals, is left blank. last_date TRANSDATE date Date of the last action on the record (system generated).

docs.title: Parties
docs.text: Column IDB field Type Description us_appellant USAPT integer 1 if the United States initiated the appeal and 0 if not. appellant APPELLAN text Name of the party who initiated the appeal (truncated to 20 characters). us_appellee USAPE integer 1 if the appeal was filed against the United States and 0 if not. appellee APPELLEE text Name of the party against whom the appeal was taken (truncated to 20 characters). pro_se_at_filing PROSEFLE integer Pro se parties at filing. See Pro se parties. pro_se_at_termination PROSETRM text Pro se parties at termination. See Pro se parties. pro_se_party PROSEFLE, PROSETRM integer Added. 1 if either column shows a pro se party (codes 1, 2, or 3), 0 if neither does, and blank if both are missing. in_forma_pauperis FILEFEE integer 1 if a party was granted permission to proceed in forma pauperis at filing (FP). The IDB stores -8 for all other appeals, which is left blank. in_forma_pauperis_termination TRMFEE text In forma pauperis status at termination: 1 if granted (FP), 0 if not (N), and Missing/Pending for -8, which appears only on pending appeals.

docs.title: Type of appeal
docs.text: Column IDB field Type Description appeal_type APPTYPE text Type of appeal at filing. See Appeal types. appeal type indicators APPTYPE integer Added. One column for each appeal type, named in Appeal types. appeal_type_termination TRMTYPE text Type of appeal as reported by the clerk at termination, using the same codes as appeal_type. It differs from appeal_type in about 0.07% of terminated appeals, almost all in 2008–2010 and among the sentencing guideline codes. It is -8 for pending appeals. appeal type indicators at termination TRMTYPE integer Added. The same indicator columns built from appeal_type_termination, each with _at_termination added to its name. For pending appeals, only appeal_type_missing_at_termination is 1. writ ORGPROC integer Nature of an original proceeding (coded only when appeal_type is 6). See Writs for the codes. writ_termination TORPROCSUB text Nature of an original proceeding as reported at termination. See Writs. agency AGENCY text Federal agency involved in an administrative appeal (coded only when appeal_type is 1 or 2). See Agencies. Non-agency appeals (IDB code -9) are labeled None.

docs.title: Lower court
docs.text: Column IDB field Type Description circuit_of_origin DCIRC text Circuit of the district or bankruptcy court where the case was first filed. See Circuits. district_of_origin DDIST text District or bankruptcy court where the case was first filed. The IDB's two-character code is combined with the circuit to match the codebook's district list. See Districts. district_courthouse DOFFICE text Office of the district or bankruptcy court where the case was first filed, as "City, ST". See Courthouses. district_docket DDOCKET text Docket number in the district or bankruptcy court. district_docket_date DDKTDATE date Date the case was docketed in the district or bankruptcy court. appeal_date APPDATE date Date the notice of appeal was filed in the lower court. For interlocutory appeals under 28 U.S.C. § 1292(b), the date the application was granted. district_judge DJUDGE text Code of the judge whose decision was appealed. Blank in the public files. jurisdiction JURIS text Basis of federal jurisdiction in civil appeals. See Jurisdiction. nature_of_suit NOS integer Nature of the action in civil appeals. See Nature of suit. -9 for non-civil appeals. nature of suit indicators NOS integer Added. One column for each group of nature of suit codes. See Nature of suit groups. criminal_offense OFFENSE integer Offense charged in criminal appeals. Codes are stored as numbers, so leading zeros are dropped (0100 becomes 100). See Criminal offenses. -9 for non-criminal appeals. offense indicators OFFENSE integer Added. One column for each group of offense codes. See Offense groups. Blank when the offense is missing. criminal_defendant_number DDEFNUM text Defendant number in the district court for criminal cases. criminal_capital_case FEDCAP integer 1 for a federal capital case (Y), such as an appeal in which a defendant was sentenced to death, and 0 otherwise (-8).

docs.title: Disposition
docs.text: Column IDB field Type Description when_terminated DISP text How the appeal was terminated. See Termination codes. disposition OUTCOME text Outcome of an appeal decided on the merits (when_terminated 1, 2, or 3). See Termination codes. procedural_termination PROCTERM integer Type of procedural termination after judicial action (when_terminated 4). See Termination codes. non_merits_disposition METHOD text Type of termination by the clerk without judicial action (when_terminated 5). See Termination codes. original_proceeding_termination OPDISP text Outcome of an original proceeding: 1 granted, 2 denied, 3 dismissed or other. judgment_date JUDGDATE date Date the final judgment, decree, or order was entered. published_status PUBSTAT integer Type of opinion or order. See Publication. published PUBSTAT integer Added. 1 for a published opinion (codes 2, 4, 6), 0 for an unpublished one (1, 3, 5, 7), and blank otherwise, including the undocumented code 0. joined_appeal JOINAPP text Type of joined appeal: 0 none, 1 cross appeal, 2 consolidated appeal, 3 lead case of a consolidated group. joined_docket CONSDKT text Docket number (in IDB form) of the first appeal of a cross appeal or the lead case of a consolidated group. enbanc ENBANC text 1 if the appeal was heard en banc (Y), 0 if not (N), and Missing/Pending for -8, which appears only on pending appeals.

docs.title: Dates and timing
docs.text:
Column IDB field Type Description briefing_notice_date CRECDATE date Date the briefing notice or schedule was issued. Missing in every file from 2008 to 2026. brief_filed_date BRFILED date Date the last brief was received before hearing or submission. submitted_date SUBDATE date For appeals decided on the merits without a hearing, the date the appeal was submitted to the first judge on the panel. hearing_date HEARDATE date Date the appeal was argued before a panel. hearing_to_judgment HEARDATE, JUDGDATE integer Added. Days from hearing_date to judgment_date. notice_to_judgment APPDATE, JUDGDATE integer Added. Days from appeal_date to judgment_date. notice_to_hearing APPDATE, HEARDATE integer Added. Days from appeal_date to hearing_date.

Each added gap is blank if either of its dates is missing. A few gaps are negative or very long because of errors in the IDB dates.

docs.title: Panel and opinions
docs.text:
Column IDB field Type Description opinion_types OPINION text Separate opinions on the panel: 6 dissent only, 7 concurrence only, 8 both (not en banc), 9 both (en banc). judge_1, judge_2, judge_3 JDGCODE1–3 text Statistical codes of the judges on the panel. Blank in the public files. judge_1_opinion_type, judge_2_opinion_type, judge_3_opinion_type JDG1INV–JDG3INV text Each judge's role. See Judge roles. concurrences JDG1INV–JDG3INV integer Added. Number of the three judges who wrote a concurrence (roles B, D, E, or G). Blank if all three roles are missing. dissents JDG1INV–JDG3INV integer Added. Number of the three judges who wrote a dissent (roles C, F, or G). Blank if all three roles are missing.

For en banc appeals, the IDB records only three judges, so concurrences and dissents count only the opinions of those three.

docs.title: Civil District Codebook
docs.text: This codebook describes the civil CSV file that fjc-idb creates from the FJC Integrated Database (IDB) files for civil cases in the U.S. district courts. It follows the FJC's Civil Documentation for 1988 forward (October 25, 2023), adapted to the column names, labels, and added columns that fjc-idb produces. The original codebook is available from the FJC IDB page.

docs.title: About the data
docs.text:
• One row per case. Each row is a civil case. The district, office, and docket number together identify a case; a case that is reopened, remanded, or transferred can appear again with a new row.
  • Years. The IDB has one file for each statistical year, which runs from October 1 through September 30. Each file holds the cases terminated that year. The most recent files also hold a snapshot of cases still pending when the file was made.
  • Pending cases. A pending case is repeated in each file until it ends, so fjc-idb keeps pending cases only from the latest file in the range. In those rows, pending is 1 and data_file_year is 2099.
  • Records are updated. Each record reflects the case as of the latest update the FJC received, so information that changed during the case (such as pro se or in forma pauperis status) can be overwritten.
  • Column order. The CSV keeps the order of the original file, with each added column placed next to the column it comes from. The tables below group the columns by subject instead.

docs.text: Topic How fjc-idb handles it Column names Each original IDB field is renamed to a descriptive name. Pass rename_columns=False (or --rename-columns false) to keep the IDB names, such as PROCPROG. Missing data The IDB code -8 and the date 1900-01-01 mean missing data. They are written as NA in date columns and left blank in all other columns, unless a column below says otherwise. Labels Columns marked with a label table have their codes replaced by labels. docs.title: Criminal District Codebook
docs.text: This codebook describes the criminal CSV file that fjc-idb creates from the FJC Integrated Database (IDB) files for criminal defendants in the U.S. district courts. It follows the FJC's Criminal Integrated Database (IDB): 1996 to Present codebook (August 2016), adapted to the column names, labels, and added columns that fjc-idb produces. The original codebook is available from the FJC IDB page.

docs.title: About the data
docs.text:
• One row per defendant. Unlike the civil and appellate files, each row is a defendant, not a case. A case with several defendants has several rows, identified by defendant_number or defendant_key.
  • Years. The IDB has one file for each fiscal year, which runs from October 1 through September 30. Each file is a snapshot with one record for every defendant filed or terminated during the year, or still pending at its end. A record holds both the filing and, once the defendant is terminated, the closing data. The record is the most recent one the court sent, so earlier information (such as the charges in a superseded indictment) can be overwritten.
  • Pending defendants. A pending defendant is repeated in every file until terminated, so fjc-idb keeps pending defendants only from the latest file in the range. In those rows, pending is 1 and data_file_year is 2099. A defendant terminated in one year and terminated again in a later year (for example, after a retrial) has a row for each termination.
  • Code changes. The FJC updated the data back to 1996 to use the codes in place since fiscal year 2012. Some fields were created in 2012 and are missing or calculated for earlier years, as noted below.
  • Column order. The CSV keeps the order of the original file, with each added column placed after the columns it comes from. The tables below group the columns by subject instead.

docs.title: Conventions
docs.text: Topic How fjc-idb handles it Column names Each original IDB field is renamed to a descriptive name. Pass rename_columns=False (or --rename-columns false) to keep the IDB names, such as FOFFCD1. Missing data The IDB code -8 and the date 1900-01-01 mean missing data. They are written as NA in date columns and left blank in all other columns. Labels Columns marked with a label table have their codes replaced by labels. Codes with no label are kept as they are. Indicators Added indicator columns are 1 for yes and 0 for no. Added columns Columns marked added are created by fjc-idb and are not in the IDB. Numbered columns The IDB records up to five offenses for each defendant at filing and at termination, ranked by severity. Columns ending in _1 through _5 describe offense 1 (the most severe) through offense 5.

docs.title: Defendant and case identification
docs.text: Column IDB field Type Description fiscal_year FISCALYR integer Fiscal year of the file the row comes from. circuit CIRCUIT text Circuit where the case was located. See Circuits. The IDB stores this field as text (09); it is matched to the same labels as the other files. district DISTRICT text District where the case was located. The IDB's two-character code is combined with the circuit to match the codebook's district list. See Districts. district_courthouse OFFICE text Office where the case was located, as "City, ST". See Courthouses. docket DOCKET text District docket number: a two-digit calendar year and a five-digit sequence number. defendant_number DEFNO integer System-assigned number of the defendant in the case, which the court cannot change. court_defendant_number CTDEF integer Court-assigned number of the defendant, which the court can renumber. Missing before fiscal year 2012. defendant_name NAME text Defendant's name. Blank in the public files. reopen_sequence REOPSEQ integer 0 for an original proceeding, 1 for the first reopening, and so on. Reopenings terminated before fiscal year 2012 are all 1. case_type TYPEREG text Type of the current case. See Case types. case_type_transfer TYPETRN text Type of the originating case, if the case was transferred. case_type_magistrate TYPEMAG text Type of the magistrate judge case, if the case was merged from one. defendant_key DEFLGKY text Unique key for the defendant: district, office, docket number, case type, defendant number, and reopen sequence. case_key CASLGKY text Unique key for the case: district, office, docket number, case type, and reopen sequence. magistrate_docket MAGDOCK text Docket number of a magistrate judge case later merged into the criminal case. magistrate_defendant_number MAGDEF integer Defendant number in that magistrate judge case. county COUNTY text Five-digit FIPS code of the county where the offense was committed (two digits for the state and three for the county). 88888 means outside the home state and 99999 outside the United States.

Column IDB fields Type Description offense indicators D2FOFFCD1–5 integer Added. One column for each group of offense codes, which is 1 if any of the defendant's five filing offenses is in the group. The same columns built from the five termination offenses, each with _at_termination added to its name. Blank for defendants who have not been terminated.

def create_folders(
    data_folder: str | pathlib.Path = options._DATA_FOLDER,
) -> list[pathlib.Path]:
    """Creates the folders of the data folder that do not exist yet.

    The data folder gets a folder for the yearly files of each case type and a
    'docs' folder for the codebooks. Folders that already exist, and the files
    in them, are left as they are.

    Examples:

Files are saved under their FJC names (such as 'ap12_0.sas7bdat') in the folder that run reads for case_type. A year that already has a file is skipped unless overwrite is True, in which case its file is replaced. The FJC updates the file for the current year during the year, so overwrite it to get the latest data. Years the FJC has not published are skipped with a warning. Any folders of the data folder that do not exist yet are created (see create_folders).

The first statistical year to download.

The last statistical year to download. Defaults to None, in which case the current year is used.

The path to the folder containing the FJC IDB dataset. Defaults to options._DATA_FOLDER.

_DATA_FOLDER overwrite bool

Whether to replace files that already exist. Defaults to False.

False codebook bool

Whether to also download the codebook for case_type into the 'docs' folder of data_folder. Defaults to True.

>>> fjc_idb.download('appellate', 2008, 2026)
Source code in src/fjc_idb/downloader.py 
def download(
    case_type: str,
    start_year: int,
    stop_year: int | None = None,
    data_folder: str | pathlib.Path = options._DATA_FOLDER,
    *,
    overwrite: bool = False,
    codebook: bool = True) -> list[pathlib.Path]:
    """Downloads the yearly FJC IDB files for a range of years.

    Files are saved under their FJC names (such as 'ap12_0.sas7bdat') in the
    folder that `run` reads for `case_type`. A year that already has a file is
    skipped unless `overwrite` is True, in which case its file is replaced. The
    FJC updates the file for the current year during the year, so overwrite it
    to get the latest data. Years the FJC has not published are skipped with a
    warning. Any folders of the data folder that do not exist yet are created
    (see `create_folders`).

    Args:
        case_type: The source type ('appellate', 'civil', or 'criminal').
        start_year: The first statistical year to download.
        stop_year: The last statistical year to download. Defaults to None, in
            which case the current year is used.
        data_folder: The path to the folder containing the FJC IDB dataset.
            Defaults to options._DATA_FOLDER.
        overwrite: Whether to replace files that already exist. Defaults to
            False.
        codebook: Whether to also download the codebook for `case_type` into
            the 'docs' folder of `data_folder`. Defaults to True.

    Returns:
        list[pathlib.Path]: The files that were downloaded.

    Raises:
        ValueError: If `case_type` is not a recognized source type.

    Examples:
        >>> import fjc_idb
        >>> fjc_idb.download('appellate', 2008, 2026)  # doctest: +SKIP

    """
    if case_type not in options._DATASET_PAGES:
        message = (
            f'Invalid source type: {case_type}. '
            f'Must be one of {list(options._DATASET_PAGES)}.')
        raise ValueError(message)
    stop_year = stop_year or dt.datetime.now(tz = dt.UTC).year
    root = camina.pathlibify(data_folder)
    create_folders(root)
    folder = main._get_data_path(case_type, root)
    links = _get_links(options._DATASET_PAGES[case_type])
    files = _get_yearly_files(links)
    downloaded = []
    for year in range(start_year, stop_year + 1):
        if year not in files:
            logger.warning(
                'The FJC has not published a %s file for %s.', case_type, year)
            continue
        prefix = options._SOURCE_PREFIXES[case_type]
        existing = sorted(folder.glob(f'{prefix}{year % 100:02d}*.sas7bdat'))
        if existing and not overwrite:
            logger.info('Skipped %s, which already exists.', existing[0].name)
            continue
        path = _save(files[year], folder)
        # Remove an older file for the year saved under a different name.
        for file in existing:
            if file != path:
                file.unlink()
        downloaded.append(path)
    if codebook:
        codebooks = [url for url in links if '/idb/codebooks/' in url]
        for url in codebooks:
            path = root / 'docs' / _file_name(url)
            if overwrite or not path.exists():
                downloaded.append(_save(url, path.parent))
    return downloaded

def merge_district(
    start_year: int,
    stop_year: int | None = None,
    data_folder: str | pathlib.Path = options._DATA_FOLDER,
    *,
    fix_city_spellings: bool = options._FIX_CITY_SPELLINGS,
    export: bool = True) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Merges the appellate data with the civil and criminal district data.

    The appellate, civil, and criminal files for the same range of years are
    used, so an appeal can only be matched with a district case that was
    terminated in that range or was still pending. The civil and criminal files
    are read one year at a time, keeping only the records of appealed cases.

    The merged data is saved in the appellate folder as
    'fjc_idb_appellate_with_district_data_{start_year}_{stop_year}.csv'. Columns
    always have their descriptive names.

    Args:
        start_year: The first statistical year to include.
        stop_year: The last statistical year to include. Defaults to None, in
            which case the current year is used.
        data_folder: The path to the folder containing the FJC IDB dataset.
            Defaults to options._DATA_FOLDER.
        fix_city_spellings: Whether to correct misspelled city names from the
            FJC codebook. Defaults to options._FIX_CITY_SPELLINGS.
        export: Whether to save the merged data to a CSV file. Defaults to
            True.

    Returns:
        pd.DataFrame: The appellate data with the matched district columns.

    Examples:
        >>> import fjc_idb
        >>> fjc_idb.merge_district(2008, 2026)  # doctest: +SKIP

    """
    stop_year = stop_year or dt.datetime.now(tz = dt.UTC).year
    root: pathlib.Path = camina.pathlibify(data_folder)
    appellate_folder = main._get_data_path('appellate', root)
    appeals = main.parse_data(
        main.import_data('appellate', start_year, stop_year, appellate_folder),
        'appellate',
        fix_city_spellings = fix_city_spellings)
    civil = _match(
        appeals,
        _get_district_records(
            'civil', appeals, start_year, stop_year, root,
            fix_city_spellings = fix_city_spellings),
        rules.district_civil_appeal_types,
        ['docket'])
    criminal = _match(
        appeals,
        _get_district_records(
            'criminal', appeals, start_year, stop_year, root,
            fix_city_spellings = fix_city_spellings),
        rules.district_criminal_appeal_types,
        ['docket', 'defendant_number'])
    added = _get_added_columns(civil, criminal)
    merged = appeals.join(added)
    logger.info(
        'Matched %s of %s appeals with district records.',
        merged[f'{_PREFIX}match'].notna().sum(), len(merged))
    if export:
        replacements: dict[str, Any] = {
            spec.name: spec.missing_replacement
            for spec in main._get_columns('appellate').values()}
        replacements |= {
            name: 'NA' for name in added.columns
            if added[name].dtype.kind == 'M'}
        file_name = (
            f'fjc_idb_appellate_with_district_data_{start_year}_{stop_year}'
            '.csv')
        main.export_data(merged, appellate_folder, file_name, replacements)
    return merged

def download(
    case_type: str,
    start_year: int,
    stop_year: int | None = None,
    data_folder: str | pathlib.Path = options._DATA_FOLDER,
    *,
    overwrite: bool = False,
    codebook: bool = True) -> list[pathlib.Path]:
    """Downloads the yearly FJC IDB files for a range of years.

    Files are saved under their FJC names (such as 'ap12_0.sas7bdat') in the
    folder that `run` reads for `case_type`. A year that already has a file is
    skipped unless `overwrite` is True, in which case its file is replaced. The
    FJC updates the file for the current year during the year, so overwrite it
    to get the latest data. Years the FJC has not published are skipped with a
    warning. Any folders of the data folder that do not exist yet are created
    (see `create_folders`).

    Args:
        case_type: The source type ('appellate', 'civil', or 'criminal').
        start_year: The first statistical year to download.
        stop_year: The last statistical year to download. Defaults to None, in
            which case the current year is used.
        data_folder: The path to the folder containing the FJC IDB dataset.
            Defaults to options._DATA_FOLDER.
        overwrite: Whether to replace files that already exist. Defaults to
            False.
        codebook: Whether to also download the codebook for `case_type` into
            the 'docs' folder of `data_folder`. Defaults to True.

    Returns:
        list[pathlib.Path]: The files that were downloaded.

    Raises:
        ValueError: If `case_type` is not a recognized source type.

    Examples:
        >>> import fjc_idb
        >>> fjc_idb.download('appellate', 2008, 2026)  # doctest: +SKIP

    """
    if case_type not in options._DATASET_PAGES:
        message = (
            f'Invalid source type: {case_type}. '
            f'Must be one of {list(options._DATASET_PAGES)}.')
        raise ValueError(message)
    stop_year = stop_year or dt.datetime.now(tz = dt.UTC).year
    root = camina.pathlibify(data_folder)
    create_folders(root)
    folder = main._get_data_path(case_type, root)
    links = _get_links(options._DATASET_PAGES[case_type])
    files = _get_yearly_files(links)
    downloaded = []
    for year in range(start_year, stop_year + 1):
        if year not in files:
            logger.warning(
                'The FJC has not published a %s file for %s.', case_type, year)
            continue
        prefix = options._SOURCE_PREFIXES[case_type]
        existing = sorted(folder.glob(f'{prefix}{year % 100:02d}*.sas7bdat'))
        if existing and not overwrite:
            logger.info('Skipped %s, which already exists.', existing[0].name)
            continue
        path = _save(files[year], folder)
        # Remove an older file for the year saved under a different name.
        for file in existing:
            if file != path:
                file.unlink()
        downloaded.append(path)
    if codebook:
        codebooks = [url for url in links if '/idb/codebooks/' in url]
        for url in codebooks:
            path = root / 'docs' / _file_name(url)
            if overwrite or not path.exists():
                downloaded.append(_save(url, path.parent))
    return downloaded

Imports, parses, and exports data from the FJC Integrated Database.

The FJC distributes the Integrated Database (IDB) as yearly SAS files. The functions in this module turn those files into one clean table per case type:

  • import_data reads the yearly files for a range of years and drops the outdated pending cases repeated in earlier files.
  • parse_data converts missing-value codes to missing data, replaces codes with readable labels, converts each column to its data type, adds derived columns, and renames the columns.
  • export_data writes a parsed table to a CSV file.
  • run does all three for a range of years, one yearly file at a time.

The case types are 'appellate' (courts of appeals), 'civil' (district court civil cases), and 'criminal' (district court criminal defendants).

def export_data(
    data: pd.DataFrame,
    data_folder: pathlib.Path,
    file_name: str,
    missing_replacements: dict[str, Any] | None = None,
    *,
    append: bool = False) -> None:
    """Exports the FJC IDB dataset to a CSV file.

    Dates are written as YYYY-MM-DD. Missing data is written as the value in
    `missing_replacements` for its column, or left blank.

    Args:
        data: The FJC IDB dataset to export.
        data_folder: The path to the folder where the CSV file will be saved.
        file_name: The name of the CSV file.
        missing_replacements: Values to write in place of missing data, keyed
            by column name. Defaults to None, which leaves missing data blank.
        append: Whether to add the rows to the end of an existing CSV file
            instead of replacing it. Defaults to False.

    """
    data = data.copy(deep=False)
    for name, value in (missing_replacements or {}).items():
        if name in data and data[name].isna().any():
            column = data[name]
            if column.dtype.kind == 'M':
                column = column.dt.strftime(options._DATE_FORMAT)
            data[name] = column.astype(object).where(column.notna(), value)
    output_path = data_folder / file_name
    data.to_csv(
        output_path, index = False, date_format = options._DATE_FORMAT,
        mode = 'a' if append else 'w', header = not append)

    data: pd.DataFrame,
    case_type: str,
    rename_columns: bool = options._RENAME_COLUMNS,
    fix_city_spellings: bool = options._FIX_CITY_SPELLINGS) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Parses the FJC IDB dataset.

    Missing-value codes are converted to missing data, coded columns with a
    decoder are replaced by their labels, every column is converted to its
    data type, and the days between key dates are added. Each case type also
    gets derived columns, such as indicators for groups of offenses or natures
    of suit; the codebooks in the User Guide list them.

    Args:
        data: The imported FJC IDB dataset.
        case_type: The source type ('appellate', 'civil', or 'criminal').
        rename_columns: Whether to rename columns based on the column mapping
            for `case_type`.
        fix_city_spellings: Whether to correct misspelled city names from the
            FJC codebook.

    Returns:
        pd.DataFrame: The parsed FJC IDB dataset.

    """
    specs = _get_columns(case_type)
    data = data.copy(deep=False)
    preparers = {
        'appellate': _prepare_appellate,
        'civil': _prepare_civil,
        'criminal': _prepare_criminal}
    data = preparers[case_type](data)
    if 'JURIS' in data:
        data = _parse_jurisdiction(data)
    for spec in specs.values():
        if spec.import_name in data:
            data[spec.import_name] = _parse_column(data[spec.import_name], spec)
    if fix_city_spellings:
        corrections = {
            rules.offices[code]: name
            for code, name in rules.office_spelling_fixes.items()}
        for spec in specs.values():
            if spec.decoder is rules.offices and spec.import_name in data:
                data[spec.import_name] = data[spec.import_name].replace(
                    corrections)
    data = _add_date_gaps(data)
    if rename_columns:
        data = _column_rename(data, case_type)
    return data

def parse_docket_number(docket_number: str) -> str:
    """Converts an IDB court of appeals docket number to its standard form.

    The IDB stores appellate docket numbers as a two-digit year followed by a
    serial number, with a 0 inserted before four-digit serial numbers (for
    example, '1701234' for 17-1234). The inserted 0 is removed.

    Args:
        docket_number: The docket number as it appears in the IDB.

    Returns:
        str: The docket number in the form 'No. YY-NNNN'.

    Raises:
        ValueError: If `docket_number` has fewer than six characters.

    Examples:
        >>> parse_docket_number('1701234')
        'No. 17-1234'
        >>> parse_docket_number('1910001')
        'No. 19-10001'

    """
    if len(docket_number) < _DOCKET_MINIMUM_LENGTH:
        raise ValueError(f'Invalid docket number: {docket_number}')
    year = docket_number[:2]
    docket_num = docket_number[2:]
    if len(docket_num) > _SERIAL_DIGITS and docket_num[0] == '0':
        docket_num = docket_num[1:]
    return f'No. {year}-{docket_num}'

docs.text:
Merges the appellate data with the civil and criminal district data.

An appeal from a district court case is matched with the district court's record of that case:

  • Appeals from civil cases (see rules.district_civil_appeal_types) are matched with the civil files by district and docket number.
  • Appeals from criminal cases (see rules.district_criminal_appeal_types) are matched with the criminal files by district, docket number, and defendant number. An appeal without a defendant number is matched only when the docket has a single defendant.

Reopened, remanded, and transferred cases can have several district records with the same docket number. An appeal is matched with the latest record filed on or before the notice of appeal or, if none was, with the latest record.

The district columns are added with the prefix 'district_', except those that only repeat the match keys or the appellate data (see rules.redundant_civil_columns and rules.redundant_criminal_columns). The added 'district_match' column says whether each appeal was matched with a 'civil' or 'criminal' record.

    The merged data is saved in the appellate folder as
    'fjc_idb_appellate_with_district_data_{start_year}_{stop_year}.csv'. Columns
    always have their descriptive names.

    Args:
        start_year: The first statistical year to include.
        stop_year: The last statistical year to include. Defaults to None, in
            which case the current year is used.
        data_folder: The path to the folder containing the FJC IDB dataset.
            Defaults to options._DATA_FOLDER.
        fix_city_spellings: Whether to correct misspelled city names from the
            FJC codebook. Defaults to options._FIX_CITY_SPELLINGS.
        export: Whether to save the merged data to a CSV file. Defaults to
            True.

    Returns:
        pd.DataFrame: The appellate data with the matched district columns.

    Examples:
        >>> import fjc_idb
        >>> fjc_idb.merge_district(2008, 2026)  # doctest: +SKIP

    """
    stop_year = stop_year or dt.datetime.now(tz = dt.UTC).year
    root: pathlib.Path = camina.pathlibify(data_folder)
    appellate_folder = main._get_data_path('appellate', root)
    appeals = main.parse_data(
        main.import_data('appellate', start_year, stop_year, appellate_folder),
        'appellate',
        fix_city_spellings = fix_city_spellings)
    civil = _match(
        appeals,
        _get_district_records(
            'civil', appeals, start_year, stop_year, root,
            fix_city_spellings = fix_city_spellings),
        rules.district_civil_appeal_types,
        ['docket'])
    criminal = _match(
        appeals,
        _get_district_records(
            'criminal', appeals, start_year, stop_year, root,
            fix_city_spellings = fix_city_spellings),
        rules.district_criminal_appeal_types,
        ['docket', 'defendant_number'])
    added = _get_added_columns(civil, criminal)
    merged = appeals.join(added)
    logger.info(
        'Matched %s of %s appeals with district records.',
        merged[f'{_PREFIX}match'].notna().sum(), len(merged))
    if export:
        replacements: dict[str, Any] = {
            spec.name: spec.missing_replacement
            for spec in main._get_columns('appellate').values()}
        replacements |= {
            name: 'NA' for name in added.columns
            if added[name].dtype.kind == 'M'}
        file_name = (
            f'fjc_idb_appellate_with_district_data_{start_year}_{stop_year}'
            '.csv')
        main.export_data(merged, appellate_folder, file_name, replacements)
    return merged
